stem: At what cost is closing inventory valued under absorption costing?

options.content: Full production cost with fixed overhead
options.rationale: Correct: all production costs are charged to units.

options.content: Variable production cost only, without any fixed overhead
options.rationale: That is marginal costing.

options.content: Prime cost only, without the production overheads
options.rationale: Prime cost leaves out the production overheads.

options.content: Selling price less the usual profit margin on sales
options.rationale: Inventory is valued at cost, not at a price less margin.

explanation: Absorption costing charges all production costs, fixed and variable, to units, so inventory is valued at full production cost.

stem: How are selling and administration expenses treated in an absorption costing profit statement?

options.content: As part of the cost of closing inventory
options.rationale: Only production costs are carried in inventory.

options.content: As period costs deducted in full in the period
options.rationale: Correct: they are not part of the production cost of inventory.

options.content: As part of the cost of each unit produced
options.rationale: Non-production costs are not absorbed into units.

options.content: They are ignored until the goods are sold
options.rationale: They are charged to the period in which they are incurred.

explanation: Non-production overheads are period costs. They are deducted in the period and are not included in inventory valuation.

stem: A product's full production cost is US\$30 and the owner uses a mark-up of 40% on full cost. What is the selling price?

options.rationale: This is the mark-up only, not the price.
This divides the cost by 0.6, treating 40% as a margin on price.
Correct: 30 × 1.40.
This adds 40 to the cost as a dollar amount.

explanation: Selling price = 30 + 40% × 30 = US\$42.
hints: Mark-up is a percentage of cost.

stem: A business has 600 units in opening inventory, produces 5,400 units and sells 5,100 units. How many units are in closing inventory?

options.rationale: This is the difference between production and sales and leaves out the opening inventory.
This adds the sales to the opening inventory.
This is the opening inventory; the closing inventory has changed.

explanation: Closing units = opening 600 + produced 5,400 - sold 5,100 = 900.

stem: Under absorption costing, production exceeds sales in a year and all costs and prices are unchanged. What happens to profit compared with a year in which production equals sales?

options.content: Profit is lower, because fixed overhead is charged twice
options.rationale: Fixed overhead is charged once, partly to the next period.

options.content: Profit is higher, because fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory
options.rationale: Correct: some fixed overhead is not charged to the year.

options.content: Profit is the same, because the total cost does not change
options.rationale: The cost charged to the period changes with the inventory.

options.content: Profit is lower, because inventory is valued at variable cost
options.rationale: Absorption costing values inventory at full cost.

explanation: When inventory rises, part of the fixed production overhead is carried forward in closing inventory, so less is charged to the current year and profit is higher.
hints: What happens to the fixed overhead of the unsold units?

stem: Which is a limitation of absorption costing?

options.content: It cannot value inventory for the financial statements
options.rationale: It is the method used for inventory valuation.

options.content: It ignores fixed production overhead completely
options.rationale: It includes fixed production overhead.

options.content: It cannot be used for pricing
options.rationale: Cost-plus pricing uses absorption cost.

options.content: The overhead per unit depends on the arbitrary bases chosen
options.rationale: Correct: different apportionment bases give different unit costs.

explanation: The allocation, apportionment and choice of base are arbitrary, so unit costs are estimates and may mislead short-run decisions.
hints: Think about how overheads are shared.

stem: A manager wants to refuse a special order priced above variable cost but below full absorption cost. What is the best comment?

options.content: It must be refused, because every order must cover its full cost
options.rationale: This ignores the fact that fixed costs do not change with the order.

options.content: It must be accepted, whatever the price that is offered
options.rationale: A price below variable cost would reduce profit.

options.content: It is irrelevant, because it is a one-off order from one buyer
options.rationale: One-off orders are evaluated on relevant cost.

options.content: It may add to profit, as the fixed overhead is incurred anyway
options.rationale: Correct: the fixed overhead is not avoidable in the short run.

explanation: Full absorption cost includes fixed overhead that does not change with the order. If the price exceeds the extra costs the order adds to profit, subject to non-financial factors.
hints: Which costs will change if the order is accepted?

stem: When closing inventory is higher than opening inventory, profit under absorption costing is higher than it would be if all fixed production overhead had been charged to the year.
explanation: True. Fixed overhead in the extra inventory is carried forward to the next period.

stem: Absorption costing statements must include selling expenses in the valuation of closing inventory.
explanation: False. Only production costs are included in inventory; selling expenses are period costs.

stem: Match each item to its treatment in an absorption costing profit statement.

right.content: Added to production cost in cost of goods available
Deducted to give cost of sales
Deducted in full as a period cost

explanation: Cost of sales = opening inventory + production cost - closing inventory. Under-absorption reduces profit; administration is a period cost.

stem: Complete the sentences.

payload.template: Under absorption costing, closing inventory is valued at {{blank:a}} production cost. Selling expenses are {{blank:b}} costs.

explanation: Inventory carries full production cost; selling expenses are period costs.

stem: State the method of setting a selling price by adding a percentage to the full cost of a unit.
explanation: It is cost-plus pricing.

stem: Gweru Candle Works has a full production cost of US\$7.50 a candle (direct materials US\$2.50, direct labour US\$1.50, variable overhead US\$0.50 and fixed overhead US\$3). It had 800 candles in opening inventory, produced 9,200 and sold 9,500. Calculate the value of the closing inventory at full production cost.
explanation: Closing units = 800 + 9,200 - 9,500 = 500. Value = 500 × 7.5 = US\$3,750. Valuing at variable cost only would give US\$2,250.
workedSolution: 1. Closing units = 800 + 9,200 - 9,500 = 500. Value = 500 × 7.5 = US\$3,750. Valuing at variable cost only would give US\$2,250.

stem: Using the same data and opening inventory valued at US\$7.50 a candle, calculate the cost of sales.
hints: Opening inventory + production cost - closing inventory.

stem: Fixed production overhead is absorbed at US\$3 a candle and actual fixed production overhead was US\$30,000. Calculate the under-absorbed overhead for the production of 9,200 candles.
hints: Compare actual with the amount absorbed.

stem: The selling price is US\$11 a candle. Selling expenses are US\$0.80 a candle sold and administration expenses are US\$9,000. Using your answers above, calculate the profit for the year.
explanation: Sales 104,500 - cost of sales 71,250 - under-absorbed 2,400 = gross profit 30,850. Less selling 7,600 and administration 9,000 = US\$14,250.
workedSolution: 1. Sales 104,500 - cost of sales 71,250 - under-absorbed 2,400 = gross profit 30,850. Less selling 7,600 and administration 9,000 = US\$14,250.
hints: Do not forget the under-absorbed overhead.

stem: Explain why selling and distribution expenses are not included in the valuation of inventory.

points.description: They are not costs of producing the goods but of selling them
They are period costs that belong to the period in which they are incurred, so they are deducted in full from profit

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Selling and distribution are costs of selling, not of making, the goods. They are period costs, so they are charged in the period and not carried forward in inventory.

explanation: One mark for each point.

stem: Explain how a manager could increase reported profit under absorption costing without selling more goods.

points.description: Produce more than is sold, so that inventory rises
Fixed production overhead in the extra inventory is carried forward and not charged to the year
So profit rises, although no extra goods have been sold, and the cash position may worsen

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: By producing more than he sells, closing inventory rises and part of the fixed overhead is carried forward in the inventory, so less is charged and reported profit rises. Cash is tied up in unsold goods.

explanation: One mark for each point.
hints: Where does the fixed overhead of unsold goods go?

stem: Evaluate the usefulness of absorption costing information to the owner of a small bakery.

points.description: It gives a full cost per loaf for pricing and shows whether the price covers all production costs
It values unsold stock correctly for the financial statements
Overhead per unit depends on arbitrary bases and on budgeted output, so it can mislead
It does not show which costs change with output, so it is poor for short-run decisions such as special orders
Judgement: useful for long-run pricing, but should be supported by marginal (contribution) data and non-financial factors

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Absorption cost shows what a loaf costs in full, which helps pricing and inventory valuation. However, overhead shares are arbitrary and fixed costs are hidden in unit cost, so it is unsuitable for short-run decisions. The owner needs both full cost and contribution information.

explanation: One mark for each of the five points.
hints: Give uses, limitations and a conclusion.

stem: Kwekwe Mats Ltd makes sleeping mats. Per mat: direct materials US\$3.10, direct labour US\$2, variable production overhead US\$0.90. Fixed production overhead is absorbed at US\$4 a mat (budget US\$32,000 for 8,000 mats). Actual fixed production overhead was US\$32,000. The selling price is US\$15, selling expenses US\$1.20 a mat sold and administration US\$10,500. Opening inventory was 700 mats, production 7,600 mats and sales 8,000 mats.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the number of mats in closing inventory.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the under-absorbed fixed production overhead.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit for the year.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: Prepare the absorption costing profit statement for the year.

points.description: Sales 120,000
Cost of sales 80,000 with opening and closing inventory at US\$10 a mat
Under-absorbed overhead 1,600 deducted
Selling and administration expenses deducted; profit 18,300

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
**Kwekwe Mats Ltd: absorption costing profit statement**

|  | US\$ | US\$ |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| Sales (8,000 × US\$15) |  | 120,000 |
| Opening inventory (700 × US\$10) | 7,000 |  |
| Production cost (7,600 × US\$10) | 76,000 |  |
| Closing inventory (300 × US\$10) | (3,000) |  |
| Cost of sales |  | (80,000) |
| Under-absorbed fixed production overhead |  | (1,600) |
| **Gross profit** |  | 38,400 |
| Selling expenses (8,000 × US\$1.20) |  | (9,600) |
| Administration expenses |  | (10,500) |
| **Profit** |  | 18,300 |

parts.explanation: One mark for each group of lines.

explanation: This item tests an absorption costing profit statement with under-absorbed overhead.
hints: Full cost per mat is the sum of all four elements.
Production was below the budgeted 8,000 mats.

stem: Gweru Candle Works (full cost US\$7.50 a candle including fixed overhead of US\$3, price US\$11, selling expenses US\$0.90 a candle and administration US\$8,500 a year) started trading in year A with no inventory. Budgeted and actual production were 10,000 candles in each year, so there was no under- or over-absorption. Year A: production 10,000, sales 7,500. Year B: production 10,000, sales 10,200.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the value of the closing inventory at the end of year A.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit for year A.
parts.explanation: Sales 82,500; cost of sales 56,250; selling 6,750; administration 8,500; profit US\$11,000.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Sales 82,500; cost of sales 56,250; selling 6,750; administration 8,500; profit US\$11,000.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Calculate the profit for year B.
parts.explanation: Sales 112,200; cost of sales 18,750 + 75,000 - 17,250 = 76,500; selling 9,180; administration 8,500; profit US\$18,020.
parts.workedSolution: 1. Sales 112,200; cost of sales 18,750 + 75,000 - 17,250 = 76,500; selling 9,180; administration 8,500; profit US\$18,020.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Explain how the fixed production overhead is treated in each year and why profit per candle sold is not the same in the two years.

points.description: In year A, 2,500 candles are unsold, so 7,500 of the fixed overhead is carried forward in inventory
In year B, part of that overhead is charged to cost of sales as the inventory is sold
Profit depends on the number of units sold and on how much fixed overhead is released or deferred
Profit per candle sold is therefore different although the cost per candle is the same

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: In year A the fixed overhead of 7,500 on 2,500 unsold candles is carried forward. In year B it is released as the stock is sold, together with the overhead of the current year, so the profit pattern depends on sales as well as production.

hints: Look at the fixed overhead in closing inventory.

parts.label: (e)
parts.stem: The owner proposes to produce 20,000 candles in year C, although sales will stay at 10,200, to increase profit. Evaluate the proposal.

points.description: Absorption costing would defer fixed overhead in the extra inventory and so profit would increase on paper
But cash is tied up in unsold stock and storage costs rise
The candles may become obsolete or damaged
The fixed overhead rate was based on 10,000 candles, so output of 20,000 would over-absorb overhead and the apparent profit is not real
Recommendation: do not produce for stock merely to show profit; produce to meet expected demand

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Producing 20,000 candles would defer more fixed overhead in inventory and raise reported profit, but the extra stock ties up cash, costs storage and may not sell. Over-absorption would also have to be corrected. The owner should produce to meet expected demand.

hints: Reported profit and cash are different things.

explanation: This item shows the effect of inventory changes on absorption costing profit.
hints: Closing inventory is valued at full cost.
Year B opens with year A's closing inventory.
